\begin{abstract}
We give a complete, self-contained, finite-sample account of the robustness of
the sample median against adversarial replacement contamination, together with
three independent proofs that its robustness threshold is exactly
$\lceil n/2 \rceil$.

Working with datasets as length-$n$ vectors of rationals and with contamination
measured by Hamming distance, we prove: (i) a \emph{counting stability lemma}
--- the number of entries satisfying any predicate changes by at most the
Hamming distance --- from which the entire robustness half follows in two lines;
(ii) the \emph{breakdown half}: if $2k<n$, every median of every
$k$-contamination is sandwiched between two uncontaminated observations, hence
lies in any a priori interval containing the honest data; (iii) the
\emph{sharpness half}: if $k \le n \le 2k$, overwriting the first $k$ entries
with any prescribed value $t$ makes $t$ a median. Together these give an exact
criterion --- boundedness under budget $k$ holds if and only if $2k<n$ --- and
identify the breakdown number of the median as exactly $\lceil n/2 \rceil$,
against the mean's breakdown number of $1$.

We then prove three structural theorems that explain the threshold. A
Donoho--Huber \emph{equivariance shear} shows that $\lceil n/2\rceil$ is a
universal ceiling: every translation-equivariant estimator becomes unbounded at
budget $\lceil n/2\rceil$. The \emph{lower sample median}, a genuine
single-valued equivariant estimator, attains this ceiling. A complete
computation of the \emph{order-statistic breakdown profile} shows that the
$j$-th order statistic has breakdown number exactly $\min(j+1,\,n-j)$, a concave
tent whose unique maximiser (up to the even-$n$ tie) is the median index.
Finally, a \emph{coding-theoretic bridge} identifies the breakdown threshold
with a unique-decoding radius: for $c \neq 0$ the two-word translation code
$\{x, x+c\}$ has minimum Hamming distance $n$, and the median breaks down under
budget $k$ if and only if that code fails unique decoding at radius $k$.

All results are instantiated on two measured normalised distributions arising
from three-channel count triples: a $16$-sample run and an $8$-sample run, both
with median $73/200 = 0.365$, with breakdown numbers exactly $8$ and $4$ and
explicit worst-case intervals $[0.32,0.41]$ and $[0.33,0.40]$.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} breakdown point, sample median, adversarial
contamination, Hamming distance, order statistics, translation equivariance,
unique decoding, robust statistics.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question}

A location estimator is a rule $T$ that condenses a dataset
$x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ into a single number. The \emph{finite-sample replacement
breakdown number} of $T$ at $x$, introduced by Donoho and Huber, is the least
number $k$ of entries an adversary must be allowed to overwrite --- with
arbitrary values, chosen with full knowledge of $x$ and of $T$ --- in order to
drive $T$ arbitrarily far from any preassigned bound. It is the crudest
robustness measure available: it does not quantify \emph{how much} an estimator
moves under small perturbations, only \emph{when it stops carrying any
information at all}. Its crudeness is also its virtue, because it requires no
probabilistic model whatsoever. The guarantees below are absolute, worst-case
and finite-sample; there are no asymptotics, no distributional assumptions and
no ``with high probability''.

Folklore says the mean has breakdown point $0$ and the median $1/2$. This paper
proves both statements exactly, in the strong two-sided form (a robustness half
\emph{and} a matching sharpness half with no gap between them), and then asks
the two natural follow-up questions: \emph{can any estimator do better than the
median?} (no) and \emph{why is the answer a half?} (three different reasons,
which turn out to be the same reason).

\subsection{Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A minimal combinatorial core.} The counting stability lemma
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:count}) is the only nontrivial ingredient in the robustness
  half. It is an induction on list length and makes no reference to order,
  sorting, or the real line.
\item \textbf{Two-sided exactness.} Theorem~\ref{thm:breakdown} is an
  if-and-only-if, so the threshold is not an artefact of a lossy argument.
\item \textbf{Universal optimality.} Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} shows
  $\lceil n/2\rceil$ is a ceiling for \emph{all} translation-equivariant
  estimators, and Theorem~\ref{thm:lmedbn} exhibits a concrete single-valued
  estimator attaining it.
\item \textbf{The full quantile landscape.} Theorem~\ref{thm:profile} computes
  the breakdown number of every order statistic, exhibiting the median as the
  unique maximiser of a concave profile.
\item \textbf{A bridge to coding theory.} Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} identifies
  breakdown with failure of unique decoding for the translation orbit.
\item \textbf{Instantiation on measured data.} Section~\ref{sec:data} makes all
  of the above concrete on two measured normalised distributions.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Conventions}

We work over $\mathbb{Q}$ throughout. This is not a restriction of substance ---
every argument is order-theoretic and combinatorial, and works verbatim over any
linearly ordered abelian group --- but it makes every statement a
\emph{finitely checkable} statement about exact arithmetic, with no rounding and
no floating-point pathology. A \emph{dataset} is a finite sequence
$x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{Q}^n$; we write $|x|=n$. Cardinalities
$\#\{\cdot\}$ count positions, with multiplicity.

\section{The contamination model}

\begin{definition}[Hamming distance]
For datasets $x,y$ of the same length $n$, set
$\dH(x,y) = \#\{\, i \in \{1,\dots,n\} : x_i \neq y_i \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$k$-contamination]
Given a dataset $x$ of length $n$ and a budget $k\in\mathbb{N}$, a
\emph{$k$-contamination of $x$} is any dataset $y$ with $|y|=|x|$ and
$\dH(x,y)\le k$.
\end{definition}

The model is \emph{replacement} contamination: the sample size is preserved and
the adversary substitutes values in place. Nothing is assumed about which
positions are corrupted or how the substituted values are chosen; in particular
the adversary may see all of $x$ and may know the estimator being used.

\begin{lemma}[Metric properties]\label{lem:metric}
$\dH$ is symmetric, satisfies $\dH(x,x)=0$ and $\dH(x,y)\le n$, obeys the
triangle inequality $\dH(x,z)\le \dH(x,y)+\dH(y,z)$ for datasets of equal
length, and $\dH(x,y)=0$ implies $x=y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each is a coordinatewise induction. For the triangle inequality, at each
position the indicator inequality
$[x_i\neq z_i] \le [x_i\neq y_i]+[y_i\neq z_i]$ holds by case analysis on
whether $x_i=y_i$, and the induction hypothesis handles the tails.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Splitting]\label{lem:split}
If $|a|=|b|$ then $\dH(a \frown c,\ b \frown d) = \dH(a,b)+\dH(c,d)$, where
$\frown$ denotes concatenation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $a$; equal lengths guarantee the two concatenations align position
by position.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:split} is the workhorse behind every explicit attack below: each
attack modifies a prefix or suffix of the sample, and the splitting lemma prices
it exactly.

\section{The counting stability lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Counting stability]\label{lem:count}
Let $P$ be any predicate on $\mathbb{Q}$ and let $x,y$ be datasets of the same
length. Then
\[
  \#\{\, i : P(y_i) \,\} \;\le\; \#\{\, i : P(x_i)\,\} \;+\; \dH(x,y).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on the length. For the empty dataset both sides are $0$. For a cons step
$x=(x_1,x')$, $y=(y_1,y')$, the induction hypothesis gives the bound for the
tails. If $x_1=y_1$ the head contributes the same amount to both counts and $0$
to the distance; if $x_1 \neq y_1$ the head contributes at most $1$ to the left
count and $1$ to the distance, so the inequality is preserved in all four sign
patterns.
\end{proof}

By symmetry of $\dH$ the reverse bound holds as well, so the two counts differ
by at most $\dH(x,y)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:count} is the entire mathematical content
of the robustness half: \emph{replacing $d$ entries destroys at most $d$
witnesses of any property}.

\section{Medians and the breakdown half}

\begin{definition}[Median]\label{def:median}
A rational $m$ is a \emph{median} of the dataset $x$ of length $n$ if
\[
  n \;\le\; 2\,\#\{i : x_i \le m\}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  n \;\le\; 2\,\#\{i : m \le x_i\}.
\]
\end{definition}

This is the order-statistic-free definition. For odd $n$ it determines $m$
uniquely; for even $n$ it determines a closed interval, namely
$[x_{(n/2)}, x_{(n/2+1)}]$ in terms of order statistics. We deliberately do
\emph{not} impose a tie-breaking convention: every theorem below quantifies over
\emph{all} medians of the contaminated sample, so no guarantee can be smuggled
in by a choice of convention. The predicate is decidable, so all instances on
explicit data are finite computations.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative robustness]\label{thm:quant}
Let $x,y$ have the same length $n$, let $d=\dH(x,y)$, and let $m$ be any median
of $y$. Then
\[
  n \le 2\,\#\{i : x_i \le m\} + 2d
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  n \le 2\,\#\{i : m \le x_i\} + 2d.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:count} with $P(\cdot)=(\cdot \le m)$ to obtain
$\#\{i : y_i \le m\} \le \#\{i : x_i \le m\} + d$, and combine with
$n \le 2\#\{i : y_i \le m\}$ from Definition~\ref{def:median}. The second
inequality is identical with $P(\cdot)=(m \le \cdot)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Breakdown half: the two-sided sandwich]\label{thm:sandwich}
Let $x,y$ have the same length $n$ with $2\,\dH(x,y)<n$, and let $m$ be any
median of $y$. Then there are indices $i,j$ with $x_i \le m \le x_j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:quant}, $2\#\{i : x_i\le m\} \ge n-2d>0$, so
$\{i : x_i \le m\}$ is non-empty; pick $i$ in it. Symmetrically for $j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Interval robustness]\label{cor:interval}
If in addition every honest observation lies in $[a,b]$, then $a \le m \le b$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$a \le x_i \le m \le x_j \le b$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich} and transitivity.
\end{proof}

Corollary~\ref{cor:interval} is the form used in practice: the corrupted median
cannot escape the observed range of the clean data, whatever the adversary does
with strictly fewer than half the entries.

\section{The sharpness half and the exact breakdown number}

\begin{definition}[Prefix contamination]
For a dataset $x$, a budget $k\le n$ and a target $t\in\mathbb{Q}$, let
$x^{(k,t)} = (\underbrace{t,\dots,t}_{k},\, x_{k+1},\dots,x_n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:prefix}
$|x^{(k,t)}| = n$ and $\dH(x,x^{(k,t)}) \le k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:split} applied to the split of $x$ at position
$k$: the suffix contributes distance $0$ and the prefix at most its length $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness half]\label{thm:sharp}
If $k \le n \le 2k$ then for every $t\in\mathbb{Q}$ the dataset $x^{(k,t)}$ is a
$k$-contamination of $x$ and $t$ is a median of it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Legality is Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix}. At least $k$ entries of $x^{(k,t)}$ equal
$t$, hence $\#\{i : x^{(k,t)}_i \le t\}\ge k$ and
$\#\{i : t \le x^{(k,t)}_i\}\ge k$. Since $n \le 2k$, both conditions of
Definition~\ref{def:median} hold.
\end{proof}

Note how little the attack needs: it does not look at the data, does not sort,
and does not require $t$ to be extreme. Once the adversary owns half the
positions, \emph{every} value is simultaneously a median.

\begin{definition}[Bounded median under budget $k$]
The median of $x$ is \emph{bounded under budget $k$} if there is $B\in\mathbb{Q}$
such that for every $k$-contamination $y$ of $x$ and every median $m$ of $y$ one
has $|m|\le B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Breakdown theorem: exact criterion]\label{thm:breakdown}
For every non-empty dataset $x$ of length $n$ and every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, the
median of $x$ is bounded under budget $k$ if and only if $2k<n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) All entries lie in $[-B,B]$ for $B=\max_i|x_i|$; apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:interval}.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $2k \ge n$ and a bound $B$ existed. Put
$k'=\min(k,n)$, so $k' \le n \le 2k'$ (using $n \ge 1$ and $2k\ge n$). Take
$t=|B|+1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}, $t$ is a median of the
$k'$-contamination $x^{(k',t)}$, which is also a $k$-contamination since
$k'\le k$. But $|t|=|B|+1>B$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Breakdown number]
The \emph{breakdown number} of an estimator at $x$ is the least budget $k$ at
which it is not bounded. (The failure set is upward closed, so a least element
is a genuine threshold.)
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:bn}
For every non-empty $x$ of length $n$, the breakdown number of the median is
exactly $k^{\star}(n) = \lfloor (n+1)/2 \rfloor = \lceil n/2 \rceil$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:breakdown} the failure set is $\{k : 2k \ge n\}$, whose
least element is $\lceil n/2\rceil$.
\end{proof}

The \emph{breakdown point} is $k^{\star}(n)/n \to 1/2$.

\begin{theorem}[The mean breaks at one]\label{thm:mean}
Let $\bar{x}=\frac1n\sum_i x_i$. For every non-empty $x$ and every bound $B$
there is a $1$-contamination $y$ of $x$ with $|\bar{y}|>B$. Consequently the
breakdown number of the mean is exactly $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Replace $x_1$ by $c=n(|B|+1)-\sum_{i\ge 2}x_i$; then $\bar{y}=|B|+1>B$, and the
distance is at most $1$. Conversely, under budget $0$ the only contamination is
$x$ itself by Lemma~\ref{lem:metric}, so the mean is trivially bounded; hence
the least failing budget is $1$.
\end{proof}

\section{The universal ceiling}

\begin{definition}[Translation equivariance]
An estimator $T$ is \emph{translation equivariant} if for every non-empty $x$
and every $c\in\mathbb{Q}$, $T(x_1+c,\dots,x_n+c) = T(x)+c$. $T$ is
\emph{bounded on $x$ under budget $k$} if some $B$ satisfies $|T(y)|\le B$ for
every $k$-contamination $y$ of $x$.
\end{definition}

Equivariance is the defining property of a location estimator: the answer must
not depend on the choice of origin. The mean, all order statistics, trimmed and
Winsorised means, the midrange, and maximum-likelihood location estimates are
all equivariant.

\begin{theorem}[Breakdown ceiling; Donoho--Huber shear]\label{thm:ceiling}
Let $T$ be translation equivariant, $x$ non-empty of length $n$, and $k$ a
budget with $2k \ge n$. Then $T$ is unbounded on $x$ under budget $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix a candidate bound $B$ and set $c=2|B|+1$. Let $m=n-k$ and define
\[
  y=(x_1,\dots,x_m,\;x_{m+1}+c,\dots,x_n+c),\qquad
  z=(x_1-c,\dots,x_m-c,\;x_{m+1},\dots,x_n).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, $\dH(x,y)\le n-m=k$ and $\dH(x,z)\le m=n-k\le k$, the
latter using $2k\ge n$; so both are legal $k$-contaminations. But $y$ is
obtained from $z$ by adding $c$ to \emph{every} coordinate, so equivariance
gives $T(y)=T(z)+c$. If $|T(y)|\le B$ and $|T(z)|\le B$ then
$c=T(y)-T(z)\le 2B\le 2|B|$, contradicting $c=2|B|+1$.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis $2k\ge n$ enters at exactly one point: it is what makes both
halves of the shear affordable out of a single budget $k$. That is the whole
reason the constant is $1/2$.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:ceiling}
Every translation-equivariant estimator has breakdown number at most
$\lceil n/2\rceil$ on every non-empty dataset of length $n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Optimality of the median]
The median attains the ceiling: its breakdown number is $\lceil n/2\rceil$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:bn} and no translation-equivariant estimator exceeds
$\lceil n/2\rceil$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}.
\end{corollary}

\section{A concrete single-valued optimal estimator}

Definition~\ref{def:median} makes the median a \emph{set}. One may object that
the ceiling is only interesting if a bona fide function attains it. It does.

\begin{definition}[Lower sample median]
Let $x^{\uparrow}$ denote $x$ sorted non-decreasingly. Define
$\lmed(x) = x^{\uparrow}_{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}$ ($0$-indexed), i.e.\ the
$\lceil n/2\rceil$-th smallest observation.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Sorted counting]\label{lem:sortcount}
Write $s=x^{\uparrow}$ with $0$-indexing. For $j<n$,
$\#\{i : s_i \le s_j\}\ge j+1$ and $\#\{i : s_j \le s_i\}\ge n-j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first $j+1$ entries of $s$ are all $\le s_j$ and the last $n-j$ are all
$\ge s_j$, by pairwise sortedness; counts over a prefix or suffix bound the
count over the whole list. Sorting is a permutation, so counts computed on $s$
agree with counts on $x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:lmed}
For non-empty $x$: (i) $\lmed(x)$ is a median of $x$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:median}; (ii) $\lmed$ is translation equivariant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(i) Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sortcount} at $j=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$: it gives
$\#\{i : x_i \le \lmed(x)\} \ge \lceil n/2\rceil$ and
$\#\{i : \lmed(x) \le x_i\} \ge \lceil (n+1)/2 \rceil$, both at least $n/2$.
(ii) Adding a constant is an order isomorphism, so
$(x+c)^{\uparrow}=x^{\uparrow}+c$ by uniqueness of the sorted permutation;
reading off position $\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$ gives $\lmed(x+c)=\lmed(x)+c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:lmedbn}
The breakdown number of $\lmed$ at any non-empty $x$ is exactly
$\lceil n/2\rceil$, so $\lmed$ attains the universal ceiling of
Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The upper bound is Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling} via Theorem~\ref{thm:lmed}(ii).
For the lower bound, if $2k<n$ then $\lmed(y)$ is a median of $y$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:lmed}(i) for every $k$-contamination $y$, hence is trapped in
the range of $x$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:interval}.
\end{proof}

\section{The full order-statistic breakdown profile}

Why the \emph{middle} order statistic? Let $T_j(x)=x^{\uparrow}_j$
($0$-indexed), with the index clamped to $n-1$ so that $T_j$ is total and
equivariant. The engine is a pair of \emph{converse} sandwich lemmas, which read
a bound on an order statistic off a mere count.

\begin{lemma}[Count implies upper bound]\label{lem:conv1}
If $j<n$ and $\#\{i : x_i \le t\}\ge j+1$, then $T_j(x)\le t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose $T_j(x)=s_j>t$. By sortedness every entry from position $j$ onward
exceeds $t$, so all witnesses of ``$\le t$'' lie in the prefix
$s_0,\dots,s_{j-1}$, giving $\#\{i : x_i\le t\}\le j$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Count implies lower bound]\label{lem:conv2}
If $j<n$ and $\#\{i : t \le x_i\}\ge n-j$, then $t \le T_j(x)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Dual: if $s_j<t$ then every entry in the prefix $s_0,\dots,s_j$ is $<t$, so all
witnesses of ``$\ge t$'' lie in the suffix of length $n-j-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Robustness of $T_j$]\label{thm:osrobust}
If $j<n$, $k\le j$ and $k<n-j$, then $T_j$ is bounded on $x$ under budget $k$;
indeed $T_j(y)\in[\min_i x_i, \max_i x_i]$ for every $k$-contamination $y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $m=T_j(y)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:sortcount} applied to $y$ gives
$\#\{i : y_i \le m\}\ge j+1$ and $\#\{i : m \le y_i\}\ge n-j$. Transporting both
counts back to $x$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:count} costs $k$ each, leaving
$\#\{i : x_i\le m\}\ge j+1-k>0$ and $\#\{i : m\le x_i\}\ge n-j-k>0$. So $m$ is
sandwiched between honest observations.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact profile]\label{thm:profile}
For $j<n$, the breakdown number of $T_j$ at any dataset of length $n$ is exactly
$\beta(j)=\min(j+1,\,n-j)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Boundedness for $k<\beta(j)$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:osrobust}. For unboundedness at
$k=\beta(j)$, take a candidate bound $B$ and split on which term achieves the
minimum. If $j+1\le n-j$, flood the first $j+1$ positions with $t=-(|B|+1)$:
then $\#\{i : y_i \le t\}\ge j+1$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:conv1} gives
$T_j(y)\le t<-B$. If $n-j\le j+1$, flood the first $n-j$ positions with
$t=|B|+1$: then $\#\{i : t\le y_i\}\ge n-j$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:conv2} gives
$T_j(y)\ge t>B$. Both attacks cost at most $\beta(j)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The median index is the maximiser]\label{thm:maximiser}
For all $j<n$, $\beta(j)\le\lceil n/2\rceil$, with equality at
$j=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$:
\[
  \max_{0\le j<n}\min(j+1,\,n-j)=\Big\lceil \tfrac n2\Big\rceil,
  \qquad
  \min\Big(\Big\lfloor\tfrac{n-1}{2}\Big\rfloor+1,\ n-\Big\lfloor\tfrac{n-1}{2}\Big\rfloor\Big)
  =\Big\lceil\tfrac n2\Big\rceil .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Elementary integer arithmetic: $\min(a,b)\le\lceil (a+b)/2\rceil$ with
$a=j+1$, $b=n-j$, $a+b=n+1$; substituting the median index makes the two
arguments differ by at most one.
\end{proof}

The profile $\beta$ is a discrete \emph{tent}: $\beta(0)=\beta(n-1)=1$ (the
sample extremes are exactly as fragile as the mean), $\beta$ increases by one
per step towards the centre, and peaks at the median index --- uniquely, up to
the two-way tie when $n$ is even. So the median is the unique maximiser of a
concave profile, and the value it attains coincides with the universal ceiling
of Corollary~\ref{cor:ceiling}. The two optimality statements are logically
independent (one \emph{within} the order-statistic family, one \emph{across all}
equivariant estimators) and they agree.

\section{Breakdown as a unique-decoding radius}

The number $n$ in the criterion $2k<n$ is not merely the sample size; it is a
\emph{minimum distance}.

\begin{definition}[Translation code]
For a dataset $x$ of length $n$ and a shift $c\neq 0$, the \emph{translation
code} of $x$ is the two-word code $\mathcal{C}_c(x)=\{x,\ x+c\}$, where
$x+c=(x_1+c,\dots,x_n+c)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Minimum distance]\label{lem:mindist}
For $c\neq 0$, $\dH(x,\,x+c)=n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$x_i \neq x_i+c$ for every $i$.
\end{proof}

A global shift is the maximally spread-out perturbation: it touches every
coordinate, so the translation code has the largest possible minimum distance.

\begin{definition}[Confusability]
$x$ and $x+c$ are \emph{confusable at radius $k$} if some dataset $w$ of length
$n$ satisfies $\dH(x,w)\le k$ and $\dH(x+c,w)\le k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Unique-decoding criterion]\label{thm:confusable}
For $c\neq 0$ and any $k$, the words $x$ and $x+c$ are confusable at radius $k$
if and only if $n \le 2k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) By Lemmas~\ref{lem:metric} and~\ref{lem:mindist},
$n=\dH(x,x+c)\le \dH(x,w)+\dH(w,x+c)\le 2k$.
($\Leftarrow$) Let $m=n-k$ and $w=(x_1+c,\dots,x_m+c,\,x_{m+1},\dots,x_n)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, $\dH(x,w)\le m=n-k\le k$ (using $n\le 2k$) and
$\dH(x+c,w)\le n-m=k$.
\end{proof}

This is precisely the classical unique-decoding criterion $2k<d$ for a code of
minimum distance $d$, specialised to $d=n$.

\begin{theorem}[Bridge theorem]\label{thm:bridge}
For every non-empty $x$, every $c\neq 0$ and every $k$: the median of $x$ breaks
down under budget $k$ if and only if $\mathcal{C}_c(x)$ fails unique decoding at
radius $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:breakdown} (bounded iff $2k<n$) with
Theorem~\ref{thm:confusable} (confusable iff $n\le 2k$); the two conditions are
negations of one another.
\end{proof}

The consequence is conceptual rather than merely formal. A statistician's
breakdown point and a coding theorist's decoding radius are not analogues; on
the translation code they are the same integer computed by the same inequality.
Robust location estimation \emph{is} decoding: the honest sample is the
transmitted word, the adversary is the channel, translation equivariance is the
ambiguity the code must resolve, and the median is a decoder achieving the
channel's limit.

\section{Two measured normalised distributions}\label{sec:data}

Each measurement is a triple of raw counts $(a,b,c)$ in three channels; the
recorded statistic is the normalised first coordinate $r(a,b,c)=a/(a+b+c)$.

The \textbf{16-sample run} consists of the triples
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(37,41,22),\,(35,43,22),\,(38,40,22),\,(36,42,22),\,(34,44,22),\,(39,39,22),\,(33,45,22),\,(40,38,22),\\
&(36,41,23),\,(37,40,23),\,(35,42,23),\,(38,39,23),\,(34,43,23),\,(39,38,23),\,(41,37,22),\,(32,46,22),
\end{aligned}
\]
each summing to $100$, hence the normalised readings
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{16}=(&0.37,0.35,0.38,0.36,0.34,0.39,0.33,0.40,\\
&0.36,0.37,0.35,0.38,0.34,0.39,0.41,0.32).
\end{aligned}
\]
The \textbf{8-sample run} consists of the first eight triples, giving
\[
R_8=(0.37,0.35,0.38,0.36,0.34,0.39,0.33,0.40).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Medians]
$73/200=0.365$ is a median of $R_{16}$ and a median of $R_8$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Direct count. Sorted, $R_{16}$ is
\[
0.32,0.33,0.34,0.34,0.35,0.35,0.36,0.36,0.37,0.37,0.38,0.38,0.39,0.39,0.40,0.41,
\]
so exactly $8$ of the $16$ entries are $\le 0.365$ and exactly $8$ are
$\ge 0.365$; both inequalities hold with equality. Similarly $R_8$ sorted is
$0.33,\dots,0.40$ with $4$ entries on each side. In both cases the median
interval is $[0.36,0.37]$, of which $0.365$ is the midpoint.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Ranges]
Every entry of $R_{16}$ lies in $[8/25,\,41/100]=[0.32,0.41]$, and every entry
of $R_8$ lies in $[33/100,\,2/5]=[0.33,0.40]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Robustness, 16 samples]
Let $y$ have length $16$ with $\dH(R_{16},y)\le 7$, and let $m$ be any median of
$y$. Then $0.32 \le m \le 0.41$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$2\cdot 7=14<16$; apply Corollary~\ref{cor:interval}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness, 16 samples]
For every $t\in\mathbb{Q}$, the dataset $R_{16}^{(8,t)}$ has length $16$,
satisfies $\dH(R_{16},R_{16}^{(8,t)})\le 8$, and has $t$ as a median.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} with $n=16$, $k=8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Robustness and sharpness, 8 samples]
If $\dH(R_8,y)\le 3$ and $m$ is any median of $y$ with $|y|=8$, then
$0.33\le m\le 0.40$. For every $t$, the dataset $R_8^{(4,t)}$ is a
$4$-contamination of $R_8$ with median $t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Breakdown numbers]
The breakdown number of the median is exactly $8$ on $R_{16}$ and exactly $4$ on
$R_8$; the breakdown point is $1/2$ in both cases.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[No alternative helps]
No translation-equivariant estimator is bounded on $R_{16}$ under budget $8$,
nor on $R_8$ under budget $4$. The median's tolerance of $7$ (respectively $3$)
corrupted measurements is maximal.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[The profile on the measured data]
On $R_{16}$ the $j$-th order statistic has breakdown number exactly
$\min(j+1,16-j)$, peaking at $8$ for $j=7$; on $R_8$ it is $\min(j+1,8-j)$,
peaking at $4$ for $j=3$. In particular on $R_{16}$ the sample minimum $0.32$
and the sample maximum $0.41$ have breakdown number $1$ --- exactly as fragile
as the mean.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Confusability thresholds]
For every $c\neq 0$: $R_{16}$ is confusable with $R_{16}+c$ at radius $8$ but
not at radius $7$; $R_8$ is confusable with $R_8+c$ at radius $4$ but not at
radius $3$. These thresholds coincide with the breakdown numbers above.
\end{corollary}

Everything in this section is a finite computation on the measured triples;
there is no estimation, no model and no probabilistic caveat.

\section{Algorithms}

Throughout, $n$ is the sample size.

\begin{description}
\item[A (median verification).] Given $x$ and $m$, compute
  $\#\{i : x_i\le m\}$ and $\#\{i : m\le x_i\}$ in one pass and test both
  inequalities of Definition~\ref{def:median}. Cost $O(n)$, exact rational
  arithmetic, no sorting.
\item[B (breakdown number).] By Corollary~\ref{cor:bn} the answer is
  $\lceil n/2\rceil$, an $O(1)$ formula; the interest is in certifying it.
\item[C (robustness certificate).] Given $x$ and $k$ with $2k<n$, output
  $[\min_i x_i,\max_i x_i]$ and the count-based witness of
  Theorem~\ref{thm:quant}: for a purported contaminated median $m$, check
  $2\#\{i : x_i\le m\}+2k\ge n$. Cost $O(n)$.
\item[D (optimal attack).] Given $x$, $k$ with $2k\ge n$ and a target $t$,
  output $x^{(k,t)}$, the witness of Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}. For a general
  order statistic $T_j$ under budget $\beta(j)$, flood $j+1$ positions with a
  large negative value if $j+1\le n-j$, else $n-j$ positions with a large
  positive value. Cost $O(n)$.
\item[E (order-statistic profile).] Sort once, $O(n\log n)$, then report for
  each $j$ the pair $(x^{\uparrow}_j,\ \min(j+1,n-j))$: the complete robustness
  landscape of the sample.
\item[F (confusing word).] Given $x$, $c\neq 0$ and $k$ with $n\le 2k$, output
  the word shifting the first $n-k$ coordinates by $c$: an explicit certificate
  that the two hypotheses are indistinguishable. Cost $O(n)$.
\item[G (empirical breakdown search).] For a black-box equivariant $T$,
  evaluate $T$ on the shear pair of Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} for increasing $k$
  and report the first $k$ where $|T(y)-T(z)|$ exceeds a threshold;
  Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} guarantees this fires no later than
  $k=\lceil n/2\rceil$.
\end{description}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What the model does and does not assume}

The results are worst-case and finite-sample. The adversary is omniscient, may
substitute arbitrary values, and is positionally free. There is no probability
space anywhere in the development. The price for this strength is that breakdown
is a coarse criterion: it detects total failure, not degradation. An estimator
with breakdown point $1/2$ can still be badly biased by a single moderate
outlier --- the breakdown number is a statement about boundedness, not accuracy.
A finer analysis would use the maximum-bias curve
$\sup\{|T(y)-T(x)| : \dH(x,y)\le k\}$, whose value at
$k=\lceil n/2\rceil-1$ is exactly what Corollary~\ref{cor:interval} bounds by
the sample range.

\subsection{Three proofs of the same constant}

In each explanation the sample splits into two blocks of sizes $m$ and $n-m$,
and the adversary must afford whichever block is smaller.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.28\textwidth}p{0.36\textwidth}p{0.28\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Structure & Object being split & Threshold condition \\
\midrule
Order-statistic tent & low tail of size $j+1$ vs.\ high tail of size $n-j$ &
$\beta(j)=\min(j+1,n-j)\le\lceil n/2\rceil$\\
Equivariance shear & head of size $m$ vs.\ tail of size $n-m$, translated apart &
$\min(m,n-m)\le k$, i.e.\ $2k\ge n$\\
Hamming distance & prefix corrupted towards $x$ vs.\ suffix towards $x+c$ &
$\dH(x,x+c)=n\le 2k$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

In all three the binding constraint is $\min(m,n-m)\le k$, maximised over $m$ at
$m=\lceil n/2\rceil$. The threshold is a statement about the pigeonhole geometry
of splitting a finite set in two --- which is why it is a half, and why it is
the same half every time.

\subsection{Relation to distributional breakdown}

Classically the breakdown point is often defined for $\varepsilon$-contamination
neighbourhoods of a distribution. The finite-sample replacement version used
here is sharper and more elementary: it yields exact integers rather than
limiting fractions, requires no measure theory, and applies to the dataset
actually in hand. Corollary~\ref{cor:bn} recovers the classical value $1/2$ in
the limit while giving the exact integer $\lceil n/2\rceil$ at every finite $n$
--- including the parity phenomenon that an even sample of size $n$ and an odd
sample of size $n-1$ have the same breakdown number.

\subsection{Practical reading}

The single most useful statement for a practitioner is
Corollary~\ref{cor:interval}: if fewer than half the entries are corrupted, then
every median of the corrupted data lies within the range of the clean data. It
requires only an a priori bound on the honest observations --- often available
from physical constraints, as with normalised ratios confined to $[0,1]$. The
dual statement, Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}, is equally useful as a warning: at
exactly half, no statistical sophistication rescues the estimate, because
Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} rules out every equivariant alternative
simultaneously. This is the barrier governing Byzantine-robust distributed
learning, robust sensor fusion, and consensus over reported numerical values.

\section{Future directions}

\subsection*{D1. Concave breakdown profiles for L-estimators}

\begin{conjecture}
For a weight vector $w=(w_0,\dots,w_{n-1})$ of non-negative rationals with
$\sum_j w_j=1$, the L-estimator $T_w(x)=\sum_j w_j T_j(x)$ has breakdown number
exactly
\[
  \min\{\,j+1 : w_{j'}>0 \text{ for some } j'\le j\,\}\ \wedge\
  \min\{\,n-j : w_{j'}>0 \text{ for some } j'\ge j\,\},
\]
i.e.\ the tent profile evaluated at the extreme support points of $w$.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that the proven order-statistic profile $\min(j+1,n-j)$ is
not an accident of the median but a \emph{support functional}: contamination can
only reach an L-estimator through the extremal order statistics its weights
touch, so the profile of a mixture collapses to the minimum of the profiles of
its atoms. The two converse sandwich lemmas read a bound on any order statistic
off a count alone, and summing count-based bounds is exactly what a weighted
average needs, so this is a finite-sum argument rather than a new sorting
argument. If true, it yields the breakdown numbers of the trimmed mean, the
Winsorised mean, the midhinge, and the Tukey trimean as corollaries of a single
theorem.

\subsection*{D2. Minimum-distance duality for breakdown points}

\begin{conjecture}
Let $G$ act coordinatewise on $\mathbb{Q}^n$ and let $T$ be $G$-equivariant.
Then the breakdown number of $T$ at $x$ is at most $\lceil d_G(x)/2\rceil$,
where $d_G(x)=\min\{\dH(x,g\cdot x) : g\in G,\ g\cdot x\neq x\}$ is the minimum
Hamming distance of the $G$-orbit of $x$; equality holds when $G$ acts by
translations.
\end{conjecture}

The bridge theorem already identifies the median's breakdown threshold with the
unique-decoding radius of the two-point code $\{x,x+c\}$; the translation group
is the case in which every orbit element sits at full distance $n$, and a group
with sparser orbits should cap robustness earlier and more sharply. Since $\dH$
is a genuine Hamming metric and the confusability criterion is stated for an
arbitrary shift, replacing ``shift by $c$'' by ``act by $g$'' changes only the
computation of $\dH(x,g\cdot x)$. A consequence would be a scale-equivariance
ceiling for dispersion estimators such as the median absolute deviation and the
interquartile range.

\subsection*{D3. Block-median breakdown collapse}

\begin{conjecture}
When a sample is partitioned into $b$ blocks and a median-of-medians is formed,
the breakdown number is governed by the product structure of the partition
rather than by $n$: the adversary need only capture a majority within a majority
of blocks, so the effective threshold collapses from $\lceil n/2\rceil$ towards
$\lceil b/2\rceil\cdot\lceil (n/b)/2\rceil$, asymptotically $n/4$ rather than
$n/2$.
\end{conjecture}

Making this exact --- and identifying the block sizes that minimise the loss ---
would quantify the robustness cost of the hierarchical aggregation schemes used
in distributed estimation.

\section{Summary of results}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.38\textwidth}p{0.56\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Statement & Content\\
\midrule
Counting stability & A predicate count changes by at most the Hamming distance\\
Quantitative robustness & $n\le 2\#\{x_i\le m\}+2d$ for any median $m$ of a $d$-contamination\\
Breakdown half & $2k<n$ implies the contaminated median is trapped in the clean data range\\
Sharpness half & $k\le n\le 2k$ implies any prescribed value is installable as a median\\
Breakdown theorem & Bounded iff $2k<n$; breakdown number $=\lceil n/2\rceil$\\
Mean & Breakdown number $1$, for every sample size\\
Universal ceiling & Every translation-equivariant estimator fails at $\lceil n/2\rceil$\\
Attainment & The lower sample median is single-valued, equivariant and optimal\\
Order-statistic profile & $\beta(j)=\min(j+1,n-j)$, maximised at the median index\\
Unique decoding & Breakdown iff failure of unique decoding for $\{x,x+c\}$\\
Measured data & Breakdown numbers $8$ and $4$; ranges $[0.32,0.41]$ and $[0.33,0.40]$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\end{document}
